channel.title: Hedgerow Ledger
channel.description: Plain notes on how small things are paid for.

item.title: Who pays for the village well
item.description: A well is cheap to dig and dear to keep. This issue follows the bucket.
item.dc:creator: The Ledger
item.content:encoded:
A well is cheap to dig and dear to keep. The digging happens once, with a crowd and a picnic; the keeping happens every week, with nobody watching. This issue follows the bucket from the first stone to the hundredth repair.

Start with the rope. A rope wears where it rubs the lip of the well, and it wears faster in a dry summer, when the water is low and every pull is longer. Someone has to notice the fraying before it parts, and that someone is rarely the person who paid for it.

The keeping is the cost

Most shared things are funded like the digging and spent like the keeping. A grant, a drive or a generous neighbour covers the start. After that the cost arrives in small, dull pieces that no one wants to put their name to: a new pulley, a cleaned trough, a lid that keeps the leaves out.

The villages that keep their wells longest tend to write the keeping down. Not in a grand charter; in a notebook by the gate, where each repair and its price is listed beside the name of whoever did it. The notebook does two things at once. It shows that the well costs something every year, and it shows who has been carrying that cost.

A thing everyone uses and no one tends is not free. It is being paid for by whoever tends it, until they stop.

None of this needs money to change hands. It needs the cost to be visible, so the people drawing water can see it and take a turn. Next issue: the same question for the footbridge, which is worse, because a footbridge fails all at once.

item.title: The footbridge fails all at once
item.description: Some shared things wear out slowly. A footbridge does not.
item.dc:creator: The Ledger
item.content:encoded:
Some shared things wear out slowly and tell you so. A well rope frays, a path grows ruts, a fence leans. A footbridge does not. It looks the same on the day before it fails as it did the year it was built, and then one spring it is in the stream.

That makes it the hardest case for a village notebook. There is nothing to write down until it is too late, unless someone goes looking: lifting a plank, pressing a thumb into a beam, checking the bolts after the floods. The cost of a footbridge is mostly the cost of looking.

Paying for looking

Looking is easy to skip because it usually finds nothing. The years it finds nothing feel like wasted afternoons. The one year it finds a soft beam is the year it pays for every other, but nobody remembers the afternoons that led there.

The places that do this well turn the looking into a habit with a date on it. The first dry Saturday after the spring floods, two people walk the bridge and write one line in the notebook, even when the line is only that nothing was wrong. A row of dull lines is the record that the bridge was being kept.

It is not a satisfying thing to fund. There is no ribbon to cut. But a bridge that is looked at once a year will usually tell you, a season or two ahead, that it needs a new beam, and a beam is much cheaper than a bridge.

item.title: A note on this newsletter
item.description: How often it arrives, and why it is free.
item.dc:creator: The Ledger
item.content:encoded:
This newsletter arrives every other Friday, or less often when there is nothing worth saying. Each issue takes one small shared thing and asks who pays to keep it, in money or in time, and how they could be seen doing it.

It is free to read and will stay that way. The archive is open, and the feed carries every issue in full, so it can be read in whatever reader you prefer, offline, without an account and without anyone counting the opens.

If an issue is useful, the best thanks is to pass it to whoever keeps the well in your own street.
